findings.description: The fence closer accepts any line that starts with a matching-character run of sufficient length, regardless of what follows the run. Per CommonMark, a closing fence may only be followed by spaces/tabs — a run followed by an info string or other text remains fence content, not a valid closer. An operator demonstrating fence-and-heading syntax under Priorities with trailing text on a 'closing' fence line (e.g. `~~~ end of example`) would have the fence close early, letting a `## Destination` inside the intended demonstration start a real section and leak into every session's context.

The conductor's context.md inserts the brief with `brief.trim()`, so two briefs differing only in leading/trailing whitespace of the whole file produce identical conductor context.md. Because the conductor's hash omits a separate `brief` term and relies on `files` covering 'every word of it' (per the comment above the hash), such briefs collide on the conductor hash — contradicting that comment's promise, even though the session hash (which hashes the raw `brief`) does catch the same edit.

`SECTION_HEADING` requires `^##` with no leading whitespace, but CommonMark allows an ATX heading indented 0-3 spaces. An operator who writes `   ## Destination` (indented) has the conductor still receive the whole brief verbatim (unaffected, since `brief.trim()` only strips whole-string edges) but `workerBrief` produces no sections at all — the session gets nothing under `## Project brief`, silently, with no signal to the operator that their heading isn't reaching sessions.

New prose in this file's `pup brief` documentation uses em/en dashes, which this review's standing house-style rule (`.claude/agents/review-docs.md`) flags for text the change adds — even though historical repo prose uses them freely and CLAUDE.md/docs/conventions are silent on it.
The new 'Project brief (decision 57)' section uses em/en dashes throughout, flagged per the standing house-style rule in `.claude/agents/review-docs.md` for newly added prose.

refuted_findings.description: Symlink-following in readBrief and ensureBrief allows a session to redirect the operator's brief read/write to an arbitrary filesystem path via a planted symlink at ~/.pupitre/<id>/brief.md, exfiltrating or overwriting operator-readable/writable files (e.g. SSH keys).
refuted_findings.refutation: The validator confirmed the missing lstat check is real and matches decision 51's precedent (assertIndexIsOwnedBy in codegraph.client.ts), but refuted the security escalation: the generated bash-guard hook (buildBashGuardScript in profile-compiler.service.ts, lines 212-226) only blocks writes matching `.claude/`, and decision 36 confirms the session shell itself is unconfined by design — a session already has unrestricted read/write to any operator-accessible path via plain `cat`/`echo >`, no symlink trick needed. Decision 57's own 'Ceilings, stated plainly' paragraph already declares this exact class of gap (store-resident file reachable from a session's shell, guarded only at the CLI verb, sandbox named as the instrument) as an accepted, documented ceiling. The symlink path grants no capability beyond what a session's unconfined bash already has, so treating this as a new HIGH-severity vulnerability misstates the risk against the code and the PR's own declared threat model.
